candidate.blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort → Mobility/Immobility and Rest/Sleep: assist clients to maintain or improve activity within tolerance, provide measures that promote rest and comfort, and adapt daily care to functional limitations and client needs.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — balancing activity and rest in chronic heart failure
candidate.educational_objective: Teach a client with stable heart failure to pace daily activity by alternating manageable activity with rest, progressing activity within the individualized plan, and stopping when clinically important exertional warning symptoms occur.

options.A: Break activities into manageable periods, schedule rest between tasks, and increase activity gradually within the individualized plan while stopping for warning symptoms such as unusual shortness of breath or dizziness.
options.B: Avoid routine physical activity altogether because rest is the primary way to prevent heart-failure symptoms from worsening.
options.C: Complete all strenuous tasks in one session and continue through fatigue so activity tolerance improves more quickly.
options.D: Ignore new exertional symptoms as long as the client is able to finish the planned activity.

candidate.rationale: Current American Heart Association guidance for people with heart failure supports regular physical activity that is individualized to the client's condition and also recommends planned rest so clients do not overdo activity. AHA exercise guidance identifies dizziness, unusual or extreme shortness of breath, marked fatigue, angina, and abnormal heartbeat as warning signs that should prompt stopping activity and contacting the health care professional. The AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline further supports exercise training in medically stable clients with heart failure because it improves functional status, exercise performance, and quality of life. Therefore, A best combines activity with planned rest and symptom-guided safety. B promotes unnecessary inactivity, while C and D disregard warning symptoms.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Directly supports individualized physical activity, planned rest to avoid overexertion, gradual/structured activity participation, and stopping for clinically important warning symptoms rather than complete inactivity or pushing through symptoms.
candidate.source_document_title: Lifestyle Changes for Heart Failure; Develop a Physical Activity Plan for You; 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
candidate.source_locator: AHA 'Lifestyle Changes for Heart Failure' → 'Be physically active': activity type and amount depend on heart health and should be individualized; 'Get enough rest': schedule daily rest/relaxation to avoid overdoing activity and ease fatigue. AHA 'Develop a Physical Activity Plan for You' → 'Watch for warning signs': dizziness/lightheadedness, unusual or extreme shortness of breath, excessive fatigue, angina, and fast/uneven heartbeat warrant stopping activity and contacting the health care professional. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline → Section 7.1.3, Management of Stage C HF: Activity, Exercise Prescription, and Cardiac Rehabilitation: exercise training in medically stable HF improves functional status, exercise performance, and quality of life; activity/exercise should be individualized.
candidate.source_organization: American Heart Association; American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/Heart Failure Society of America
candidate.source_version_date: AHA lifestyle guidance current 2026; physical-activity guidance last reviewed 2024-04-24; HF guideline 2022-04-01
candidate.stem: A client with stable chronic heart failure says, "I get tired when I try to finish all of my household tasks at once." Which teaching by the nurse is most appropriate?
